extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, policymakers, and researchers interested in free speech, censorship, and related law/policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the distinct legal, moral, institutional, and technical criteria used to limit, evaluate, or govern freedom of speech across media and jurisdictions. Includes doctrinal principles (harm/offence), procedural restrictions (time/place/manner), internet-specific issues, and jurisdictional examples (blasphemy, hate-speech laws, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations to freedom of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Most legal systems generally set limits on it, particularly when it conflicts with other rights and protections, such as in cases of libel, slander, pornography, obscenity, fighting words, and intellectual property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some limitations to freedom of speech may occur through legal sanction, and others may occur through social disapprobation. Examples cited include libel, slander, pornography/obscenity, fighting words, and restrictions grounded in intellectual property law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, place, and manner restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations based on time, place, and manner apply to all speech, regardless of the view expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These restrictions are generally intended to balance other rights or a legitimate government interest. Example: prohibiting a noisy political demonstration at a politician's home at night (impinging neighbors' quiet enjoyment) while permitting a similar activity at a different time or place; funeral protests are complex and often regulated on a state-by-state basis in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of free speech principles to the Internet
rubrics_metrics.description: International, national and regional standards recognise that freedom of speech, as one form of freedom of expression, applies to any medium, including the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions (e.g., Reno v. ACLU) and commentators emphasize that the Internet is a speech-enhancing medium and that governmental regulation should stop at the traditional line of unprotected speech. Governments can continue to protect children via enforcement of existing laws criminalizing obscenity and child pornography and via public education. The Internet's 'chaos' is characterized as both a strength and a regulatory challenge; international declarations (WSIS) reaffirm the right to seek, receive and impart information through any media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm principle (John Stuart Mill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill argued that legal penalties should be based on the harm principle: freedom of expression should be curtailed legally only where it causes harm to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill's position supports the 'fullest liberty' of expression to push arguments to their logical limits; he does not support legal penalties unless they are grounded in the harm principle. The harm principle sets a high bar for legal restriction and is cited as a central defense of free speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offence principle (Joel Feinberg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feinberg introduced the 'offence principle': criminal prohibition can be justified if it would probably be an effective way of preventing serious offence to persons other than the actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feinberg argues that because offence is less serious than harm, penalties should generally be lower for offence than for harm. Factors to consider when applying the offence principle include the extent, duration and social value of the speech, the ease with which it can be avoided, the motives of the speaker, the number of people offended, the intensity of the offence, and the general interest of the community at large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content viewed as harmful or dangerous (false/dangerous speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some views are illegal to express because they are perceived to be harmful to others — this category often includes speech that is both false and potentially dangerous, such as falsely shouting 'Fire!' in a theatre and causing a panic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifications for limiting speech often reference the harm principle or the offence principle. The degree to which speech may be limited for harm or offence is culturally and politically relative; examples include laws against Holocaust denial in many European countries and other jurisdictions that criminalize specific forms of dangerous falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation and 'fake news' regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars debate regulation of disinformation: some argue more and better speech should counter misinformation, while others (e.g., Tim Wu) note that internet-era attention scarcity changes the calculus and invites new regulatory concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns about disinformation include techniques that target listeners (troll armies, flooding) and weaponize information to confuse or demoralize. The EFF warns that censorship cannot be the only answer and tech companies have a history of overcorrecting. Examples include Russian 'fake news' laws imposing prison sentences and large-scale prosecution for spreading false information about military operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blasphemy laws and apostasy restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries, blasphemy is a crime and apostasy is restricted; blasphemy laws and penalties vary widely by jurisdiction (death sentences, prison, fines, or other restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: defaming Muhammad is not protected as free speech in Austria, while France protects disparagement of Muhammad under free speech law. Apostasy has been instrumentalized to restrict freedom of speech in some countries. Maps/lists (by jurisdiction) show variation in penalties and presence/absence of blasphemy laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lèse‑majesté laws (insulting the state or monarch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries criminalize speech deemed insulting to a reigning monarch or the state (lèse‑majesté).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such expression may constitute a criminal offence in jurisdictions with lèse‑majesté laws; maps show countries with such laws as of given dates and legal penalties vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hate speech and Holocaust/Genocide denial laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of hate speech varies by country: in the United States hate speech is broadly protected by the First Amendment (R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul) except in cases of imminent lawless action, while many European countries criminalize Holocaust denial and some countries criminalize Armenian genocide denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictional differences are emphasized — what is protected in one country may be illegal in another. The page lists many European countries that outlaw Holocaust denial and notes U.S. Supreme Court precedent protecting most hate speech absent imminent violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional speech codes and public-institution policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain public institutions may enact policies restricting the freedom of speech, for example speech codes at state-operated schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such institutional restrictions can supplement or diverge from national constitutional protections; the article notes research on political differences, in-group favoritism, content moderation, and possible political bias in judicial evaluations of free speech disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual property and commodification of information as limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The public domain is under pressure from the 'commodification of information' as information with previously little or no economic value acquires independent economic value via intellectual property, contract, broadcasting and telecommunications law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commodification of factual data, personal data, genetic information and ideas through IP and contract law can restrict the free flow of information and thus function as a de facto limitation on freedom of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Internet censorship mechanisms and implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet censorship in practice can be implemented via network-level mechanisms (firewalls, proxy servers, DNS poisoning) and a wide variety of laws and administrative regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'Great Firewall of China' blocks content by preventing IP routing, uses firewall/proxy servers at gateways, and selectively engages in DNS poisoning. Implementation often involves provincial branches of state-owned ISPs and companies; governments may have many regulations directed at the Internet and vigorous technical enforcement even where systematic human review is impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-legal social limitations (deplatforming, social disapprobation, cancel culture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some limitations to freedom of speech arise through social disapprobation and private action rather than legal sanction — e.g., deplatforming, ostracism, cancel culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These social mechanisms can suppress or chill speech even without state action. The article references terms such as deplatforming, cancel culture, social rejection, and the chilling effect; it situates social sanctions alongside legal sanctions as mechanisms that limit expression.
